q: A job appends 10 files to a Delta table and crashes after 7 of them, before its commit. What do readers see?
o: 7 of the 10 files
Nothing new: the table is unchanged
An error until the files are deleted
All 10 files once the job is restarted
e: Atomicity: data files become part of the table only when the commit file lists them. Without a commit the 7 files are orphans that readers ignore.

q: An `INSERT` of 1,000 rows into a table with `CHECK (quantity > 0)` contains one row with quantity 0. What happens?
o: 999 rows are inserted and one is skipped
All 1,000 rows are inserted with a warning
The whole INSERT fails and no new version is created
The bad row is inserted with quantity NULL
e: Consistency and atomicity together: constraints are checked before the commit, and a failed check rejects the whole write.

q: A report sums account balances while an `UPDATE` moves money between two accounts. Which ACID letter guarantees the report never shows a total that never existed?
o: Atomicity
Consistency
Durability
Isolation
e: Isolation: the report reads one snapshot (one version) from start to end, so it sees either all of the update or none of it.

q: A notebook's `INSERT` returned success, then the cluster crashed a second later. Is the inserted data safe?
o: Yes: the data files and the commit were already written to cloud storage
No: it was still in the cluster's memory
Only if the table has a checkpoint
Only if the disk cache was enabled
e: Durability: a Delta write returns only after its commit file exists in object storage, which is replicated and independent of the cluster.

q: Why can a plain Parquet folder not give you consistency?
o: Parquet files cannot store types
Nothing checks a new file against the existing schema or rules before it becomes visible
Parquet files are too large
Spark cannot read more than one Parquet file
e: In a folder, any file that lands there is part of the data. Delta adds a commit step where the schema and constraints are checked first.
